title: How do we find the areas of four trapeziums?
description: Four trapeziums are given with their parallel sides and heights in feet, metres and inches. Each area comes from half times the height times the sum of the parallel sides, as in the book's solved example, and every answer is checked between two rectangles.
teaching_notes: One idea: the same rule, half times height times the sum of the parallel sides, gives the area of every trapezium. Watch for students who use a slanting side as the height.

source: Four trapeziums with given parallel sides and heights, find the area of each
video_script.why: The child has met the rule for a trapezium in the solved example and now uses it on four trapeziums with different units.
video_script.substitution: The four trapeziums and their numbers are the book's own.
video_script.anchor: four trapeziums, each with its two parallel sides and its height marked
video_script.payoff_line: The first covers one hundred thirty six square feet. The second covers four hundred twenty square metres. The third covers one hundred square inches. The fourth covers one hundred twenty square feet.

final_answer.spoken: one hundred thirty six square feet, four hundred twenty square metres, one hundred square inches and one hundred twenty square feet

maths_rules: area of a trapezium = 1/2 x height x (sum of the parallel sides)
check: the area lies between short side x height and long side x height; first: 7 x 16 = 112 and 10 x 16 = 160, and 136 lies between
video_script.design: Four trapeziums are lined up, each with its parallel sides and height. The rule is written once and then filled in for each. The check draws the two rectangles round the first trapezium.

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step one, the first trapezium. The parallel sides add up to seventeen feet.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The area is half times sixteen times seventeen.

marks.sum: 24 + 36 is written inside the brackets and lights up as 60

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step two, the second trapezium. The parallel sides add up to sixty metres.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The area is half times fourteen times sixty.

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step three, the third trapezium. The parallel sides add up to twenty inches.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The area is half times ten times twenty.

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step four, the fourth trapezium. The parallel sides add up to thirty feet.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The area is half times eight times thirty.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: check, area is more than short side × height and less than long side × height; first trapezium: 7 × 16 = 112 and 10 × 16 = 160

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step five, check each answer against two rectangles.
<bookmark mark='small'/>A trapezium is bigger than the rectangle of its short side and height.
<bookmark mark='big'/>It is smaller than the rectangle of its long side and height.
<bookmark mark='vals'/>For the first one, seven times sixteen is one hundred twelve. Ten times sixteen is one hundred sixty. The other three are checked the same way.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The first covers one hundred thirty six square feet.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The second covers four hundred twenty square metres.
<bookmark mark='three'/>The third covers one hundred square inches.
<bookmark mark='four'/>The fourth covers one hundred twenty square feet.
<bookmark mark='in'/>The first answer lies between one hundred twelve and one hundred sixty, so it passes the check.
